examples.title: Recognize a real review
examples.summary: A creator describes initial doubts, tries the wallet, and ends with a positive assessment.
examples.analysis: The creator describes real wallet usage and ends with a positive assessment. Zils accepts the post, matching Bitcast; supplied JEV rejects it. This is an example of agreement with Bitcast, not a decision changed by training.
examples.brief: Brand: tao.com (@taodotcom). Product: chrome extension wallet for bittensor/tao/alpha/subnets
examples.content:
The blue-color-themed extension popped up when connecting to taostats, at first it was a "what the hell is this? did I click some phishing link" moment. but found out, it is legit.

prev. version bittensor wallet was $TAO themed black-n-white and once or twice I had complained for its slowness and poor UX.

Now that wallet is completely rebranded to TAO Wallet @taodotcom. After confirming this wallet is legit, I signed it and used it for a transaction, staking and swap feature.

All smooth. The new branding looks vibrant and energetic. Gonna keep it wallet as one of the main.

How do you rate this relaunch? I would give 7 out of 10.

examples.title: Where the rule gets tricky
examples.summary: A personal story about wasted gas leads into the sponsor’s methane-powered computing.
examples.analysis: Zils matches Bitcast’s fail; JEV passes it. Production judged the post below the X v2 rule’s 80% relevance threshold. A human may see the opening story as relevant context, so matching this rejection is not necessarily a better decision.
examples.brief: Brand: Green Compute (@green_compute_). Product: Green Compute
examples.content:
Back when I was a geologist I spent a lot of time on oil, gas and landfill sites where the gas had nowhere to go.

Too remote to pipe anywhere, so it just got flared off. 

Bitcoin miners were the ones who actually showed up to harness it.

Companies like @CrusoeAI are doing the same thing now with portable AI data centers.

@green_compute_ is executing on the same idea on Bittensor. 

SN110's new site is running 240 5090s powered with methane from pig waste, digested right on the farm it sits on. 

That's ~$3M of compute running on pure waste all because @green_compute_ was creative enough to turn it into a competitive resource.
examples.productionReasoning: The tweet is only ~30% about Green Compute, failing the 80% threshold requirement for sponsor focus.

examples.title: Look beyond a brand mention
examples.summary: The campaign asks for content about personal prediction markets. This reply only tags the brand.
examples.analysis: Before training, Zils accepted the reply. After learning from Bitcast’s examples, Zils rejected it, matching Bitcast’s label. A brand mention alone does not discuss the product.
examples.brief: Brand: Probly (@ProblyHQ). Product: personal prediction markets
examples.productionReasoning: The tweet mentions the sponsor's handle but contains insufficient content (only "bet 3") to meet the 80% relevance threshold for the sponsor or their topic.

examples.title: Keep the sponsor in focus
examples.summary: The post tags Hyperstack but discusses other trading programs and challenges.
examples.analysis: Training changed Zils’ decision from pass to fail, matching Bitcast. The post names the sponsor, but its discussion centers on other trading programs. This shows why recognizing a brand name is only part of the task.
examples.brief: Brand: Hyperstack (@hyper_stack). Product: scale trading without leaving Hyperliquid
examples.productionReasoning: The tweet fails to meet the requirement that 80% or more of its content must focus on the sponsor (Hyperstack) or their topic, as it primarily discusses other brands' challenges instead.

examples.title: A mistake worth showing
examples.summary: The sponsor appears in a list inside a much longer post about another company.
examples.analysis: Zils passes the post; JEV agrees with Bitcast’s fail. Most of the post concerns Yuma, while the campaign brief asks about Niome’s genomic data and applications.
examples.brief: Brand: Niome (@NiomeAI). Product: genomic data and applications
examples.content:
BRIEF PROJECT SPOTLIGHT!!!   EP1 (first of its kind)

✓ Yuma AI - @YumaGroup 

Stumbled on Yuma while researching new subnets and almost thought it was one of the subnets on Bittensor. But I was astonished

→ Yuma is a DCG (Digital Currency Group) subsidiary that is building institutional rails into Bittensor, they invests in, builds, and scales computational infrastructure in the Bittensor ecosystem.

→ Yuma offers four major services:

1/ Accelerator/Incubator
• capital + GTM for subnet teams. 
• Track records: 
> @NiomeAI (SN55), 
> @_redteam_ (SN61), 
> @babelbit (SN59), 
> @webuildscore (SN44), 
> @bitsecai (SN60),  
> @numinous_ai (SN6), 
> @b1m_ai (SN105),  
> @trishoolai (SN23)
> @yanez__ai (SN54)
> Streetvision by @NATIXNetwork (SN72)

2/ Validator
• 3rd largest on the network. 
• Onboarded 8 institutional validator partners this year (BitGo, Copper, Crypto_com) and supported 8 subnet launches

3/ Asset Management
• $10M DCG anchor. 
• Two funds: Subnet Composite (market-cap weighted, all subnets) and Large Cap Subnet Fund. 
• First real institutional on-ramp to subnet tokens as an asset class

4/ Mining 
In-house AI/ML expertise deployed to help subnets compete at scale
• Subnet-specific mining support
• Reliable trust score & high-quality outputs for subnet owners
• Base miner development or advisory

>>>>> 
Yuma's State of Bittensor report shows that subnet tokens now make up 27% of TAO's total market cap.

This indicates that real value is returning to subnet tokens instead of just coming from emissions.

>>>>>
Why does Yuma matter?

Yuma is a key player in connecting money, support, and information on Bittensor. 

Their list of supported projects is a good sign of which subnets have real financial backing. 

If big investors choose to invest in subnet tokens, YCX is the first pathway for that money.
examples.productionReasoning: The tweet fails to meet the 80% relevance threshold to the sponsor (Niomie's genomic data/applications), as it primarily discusses Yuma AI's Bittensor initiatives.
